paras: The Round Mountain ambush was a shooting at Round Mountain, Cherokee County, Alabama, in September 1888, in which a white man, George Whitt, and his friends were reported to have fired from ambush on five Black men, killing two and wounding three. An armed battle between the two sides followed later that night, with several people reported killed and wounded on both sides. Newspapers from New York to California ran the report as a "race war."

The Atlanta Constitution described the shooting as "a second bloody race conflict" at Round Mountain. The September reports do not describe that earlier conflict or say what work the men involved did beyond calling one of them a "colored laborer."

According to a special from Gadsden dated September 21, a fight took place on a Sunday night between Whitt and a "colored laborer." The next night, Whitt and his friends fired from ambush on five Black men, killing two and wounding the other three. Later that night some of the Black men armed themselves, and what the Constitution called "a regular battle" followed between the two parties. Several were "reported killed and wounded on both sides," but no paper gave numbers or names for that fighting.
The coverage does not report any arrests, inquest or prosecution, and none of the dead or wounded is named.

The only source was the Gadsden special, which New York's Evening World printed on September 21 as "Whites and Negroes Fighting." The next day the Sacramento Daily Record-Union carried the same text from the California Associated Press under the headline "A RACE WAR" and the subhead "Lively Shooting Between Whites and Blacks in Alabama." The Atlanta Constitution ran it on September 25 in a column of Alabama briefs, where it alone named Round Mountain and Cherokee County.

By September 29 the story had shrunk to an unlocated item "at Gadsden, Ala., a few nights ago" in "Southern Gleanings" columns printed by the Huntsville Gazette and Louisiana's St. Landry Democrat. Every version identified the white attacker by name and race, while the Black men were described only as "negroes" and a "colored laborer." No paper commented on the shooting.

Most papers gave only the Gadsden dateline, and the gleanings brief placed the fight "at Gadsden," whereas the Constitution said the special came from Gadsden and the shooting happened at Round Mountain.

bases: A white man, George Whitt, and his friends were reported to have fired from ambush on five Black men, killing two, followed by an armed battle; no custody, accusation or lynching form is reported (A3, A5).

accounts.label: Gadsden special (wire report)
accounts.gist: After a Sunday fight between Whitt and a colored laborer, Whitt and friends ambushed five Black men on Monday night, killing two and wounding three; Black men then armed themselves and a battle followed with several reported killed and wounded on both sides.

framing.detail: Northern and western papers ran the special under race-war headlines ('Whites and Negroes Fighting', 'A RACE WAR'), naming the white attacker but none of the Black victims.
The Atlanta Constitution placed it among Alabama briefs as 'a second bloody race conflict' at Round Mountain; later Southern 'Gleanings' columns cut it to an unlocated brief 'at Gadsden'.

versions.value: Gadsden (dateline; 'at Gadsden' in the gleanings brief)

conflicts.note: Gadsden appears to be the origin of the dispatch; the Constitution, which names the place, says the special came from Gadsden and the event occurred at Round Mountain.

versions.value: Sunday and Monday nights before Sept. 21

conflicts.note: No paper gives a calendar date; Sept. 21 is the dateline, and the Monday is presumably Sept. 17 but this is not stated.

set_aside: Earlier episode: week of race riots at Round Mountain, Ala., after furnace proprietor James Elliott replaced white laborers with colored laborers.
Earlier episode: white laborers dynamited Manager Elliott's house at Round Mountain furnace; governor reported the 'war' ended with arrests.
